Lennon, McCartney and Harrison, together since 1958, went through a succession of drummers before Starr joined in 1962. Manager [Brian Epstein](/wiki/Brian_Epstein "Brian Epstein") moulded them into a professional act, and producer [George Martin](/wiki/George_Martin "George Martin") developed their recordings, greatly expanding their domestic success after they signed with [EMI](/wiki/EMI "EMI") and achieved their first hit, "[Love Me Do](/wiki/Love_Me_Do "Love Me Do")", in late 1962. As their popularity grew into the fan frenzy dubbed "[Beatlemania](/wiki/Beatlemania "Beatlemania")", the band acquired the nickname **the Fab Four**. By early 1964, the Beatles were international stars and had achieved unprecedented levels of critical and commercial success. They became a leading force in Britain's cultural resurgence, ushering in the [British Invasion](/wiki/British_Invasion "British Invasion") of the United States pop market. They made their film debut with *[A Hard Day's Night](/wiki/A_Hard_Day%27s_Night_(film) "A Hard Day's Night (film)")* (1964).

A growing desire to refine their studio efforts, coupled with the challenging nature of their concert tours, led to the Beatles' retirement from live performances in 1966. In 2014, Zuckerberg purchased 700 acres of land on the Hawaiian island of [Kauaʻi](/wiki/Kauai "Kauai"). In January 2017, Zuckerberg filed eight "[quiet title](/wiki/Quiet_title "Quiet title") and [partition](/wiki/Partition_(law) "Partition (law)")" lawsuits against hundreds of [native Hawaiians](/wiki/Native_Hawaiians "Native Hawaiians") to claim small tracts of land that they owned within his acreage.[[78]](#cite_note-:0-79) Zuckerberg responded to criticisms in a [Facebook](/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") post, stating that the lawsuits were a good faith effort to pay the partial owners of the land their "fair share".[[78]](#cite_note-:0-79) When he learned that Hawaiian [land ownership law](/wiki/Property_law "Property law") differs from that of the other 49 states, he dropped the lawsuits. Zuckerberg stated that he regretted not taking the time to understand the process and its history before moving ahead.[[79]](#cite_note-80)[[80]](#cite_note-81) Eventually, an auction helped sell the pockets of land.[[81]](#cite_note-o200-82)[[82]](#cite_note-s048-83)

Zuckerberg paid $17 million (equivalent to $20,198,330 in 2025) to add 110 acres to his contentious 1,500-acre estate in [Kauai](/wiki/Kauai "Kauai"), in December 2021.[[81]](#cite_note-o200-82)

At least $145 million was spent by Zuckerberg on land in Kauai that he is developing into a massive 1,450-acre retreat that is partially gated off. In a January Instagram post, he uploaded a picture of a massive steak and joked that "of all my projects, this is the most delicious," indicating that he is rearing beer-fed Wagyu and Angus cattle on the property, involving his daughters in the process.[[83]](#cite_note-84)

Facing the [Kansas City Royals](/wiki/Kansas_City_Royals "Kansas City Royals") in the 1980 World Series, the Phillies won their first World Series championship ever in six games thanks to the timely hitting of Mike Schmidt and Pete Rose. Schmidt, who won the National League Most Valuable Player Award in 1980, also won the World Series Most Valuable Player award on the strength of his 8-for-21 hitting (.381 average), including game-winning hits in Game 2 and the clinching Game 6. This final game was also significant because it remains "the most-watched game in World Series history" with a television audience of 54.9 million viewers.[[35]](#cite_note-Sandomir-35) Thus, the Phillies became the last of the 16 teams that made up the Major Leagues from 1903 to 1960 to win a World Series.[[36]](#cite_note-BRefPS-36) Carlton captured his third NL Cy Young Award with a record of 24–9.

With an estimated population of 587,618 as of 2024,[[2]](#cite_note-auto-3) Wyoming is the [least populous state](/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population "List of U.S. states and territories by population") despite being the [tenth-largest by area](/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_area "List of U.S. states and territories by area"), and it has the [second-lowest population density](/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_by_population_density "List of U.S. states by population density"). The [state capital](/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States "List of capitals in the United States") and [most populous city](/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Wyoming "List of municipalities in Wyoming") is [Cheyenne](/wiki/Cheyenne,_Wyoming "Cheyenne, Wyoming").[[10]](#cite_note-QF-12)

Healthcare in Canada is delivered through the provincial and territorial systems of [publicly funded health care](/wiki/Publicly_funded_health_care "Publicly funded health care"), informally called [Medicare](/wiki/Medicare_(Canada) "Medicare (Canada)").[[331]](#cite_note-337) It is guided by the provisions of the *[Canada Health Act](/wiki/Canada_Health_Act "Canada Health Act")* of 1984[[332]](#cite_note-338) and is [universal](/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care").[[333]](#cite_note-339) Universal access to publicly funded health services "is often considered by Canadians as a fundamental value that ensures national healthcare insurance for everyone wherever they live in the country".[[334]](#cite_note-340) Around 30 percent of Canadians' healthcare is paid for through the private sector.[[335]](#cite_note-Kroll2012-341) This mostly pays for services not covered or partially covered by Medicare, such as [prescription drugs](/wiki/Prescription_drug "Prescription drug"), [dentistry](/wiki/Dentistry "Dentistry") and [optometry](/wiki/Optometry "Optometry").[[335]](#cite_note-Kroll2012-341) Approximately 65 to 75 percent of Canadians have some form of supplementary health insurance; many receive it through their employers or access secondary social service programs.[[336]](#cite_note-342)
